label: Sayings LIII–LXVIII
paragraphs: LIII. No, by the gods, young man. But once you have heard these words, go away and say to yourself, "It was not Epictetus who said these things to me; where would he have got them? It was some kindly god speaking through him. For it would never have occurred to Epictetus to say these things, since he is not in the habit of speaking this way to anyone. Come then, let us obey God, so that we do not fall under his anger." No; if a raven gives you a sign by its croaking, it is not the raven that gives the sign but God through the raven. And if he gives you a sign through a human voice, will you make out that it is the man who is saying these things to you, so as to stay ignorant of the power of the divine: that it gives signs to some in this way and to others in that, and that on the greatest and most important matters it gives its sign through the noblest messenger? What else does the poet mean? "For we ourselves told him beforehand, sending Hermes, the keen-sighted slayer of Argus, not to kill the man and not to court his wife."

LIV. So my friend Heraclitus, who had a small lawsuit in Rhodes about a bit of land, after proving to the judges that his case was just, came to his closing speech and said, "But I will not plead with you, and I do not care what verdict you are going to give. It is you who are on trial rather than I." And that is how he wrecked his case.

LV. So we are in the same case as deer. When the deer are frightened by the feathers and run from them, where do they turn, and what do they retreat to as a safe place? The nets. And so they perish, having confused what is to be feared with what is safe. For it is not death or pain that is to be feared, but the fear of pain or death. That is why we praise the man who said, "It is not dying that is terrible, but dying in disgrace."

LVI. How is it, then, that some external things are said to be in keeping with nature and others against it? It is as if we were detached things. For a foot, I will say that it is in keeping with nature to be clean. But if you take it as a foot, and not as a detached thing, it will be its duty to step into mud, and to tread on thorns, and sometimes to be cut off for the sake of the whole body. Otherwise it will no longer be a foot. We should think of ourselves in some such way. What are you? A human being. If you look at yourself as a detached thing, it is in keeping with nature to live to old age, to be rich, to be healthy. But if you look at yourself as a human being and a part of some whole, then for the sake of that whole it is your duty now to be sick, now to go to sea and run risks, now to be in want, and sometimes to die before your time. Why then are you indignant? Do you not know that as the foot, detached, will no longer be a foot, so you will no longer be a human being? For what is a human being? A part of a city: first, of the city of gods and men; and then of the one that is called nearest to it, which is a small copy of the whole. For it is impossible, in such a body, in this world that surrounds us, among these companions, that such things should not happen, some to one man and some to another. Your work, then, is to come and say what you should, and to deal with these things as is fitting.

LVII. Diogenes answered well when a man asked him for a letter of introduction. "That you are a man," he said, "he will know at a glance. Whether you are a good one or a bad one he will know if he has the skill to tell good men from bad; and if he has not, he will never know, even if I write to him ten thousand times." It is as if a drachma asked to be introduced to someone so as to be tested. If he is a judge of silver, you will introduce yourself.

LVIII. What then? We should come without desire or aversion, as the traveler asks the man he meets which of two roads leads there, with no desire that it should be the right-hand road rather than the left; for he does not want to go by one of them in particular, but by the one that leads there. That is how we ought to come to God too, as to a guide; just as we use our eyes, not begging them to show us this kind of thing rather than that, but accepting the impressions of whatever they show. But as it is, we clutch the little bird, trembling, and call on God and beg him, "Master, have mercy. Let me come out of this." Slave, do you want anything but what is best? And is anything better than what seems good to God? Why do you do all you can to corrupt your judge and mislead your adviser?

LIX. God is beneficial. But the good is also beneficial. It is likely, then, that where the essence of God is, there too is the essence of the good. What, then, is the essence of God? Flesh? Far from it. Land? Far from it. Fame? Far from it. It is mind, knowledge, right reason. Here, then, and nowhere else, look for the essence of the good. For you do not look for it in a plant, do you? No. Or in a creature without reason? No.

LX. Will you not, then, look for the essence of the good in that thing without which you will not say there is good in anything else? What then? Are those other things not also works of the gods? They are, but they are not of the first rank, and they are not parts of the gods. But you are of the first rank; you are a fragment of God; you have in yourself a part of him. Why then do you not know your kinship? Why do you not know where you have come from? Will you not remember, when you eat, who you are that eat, and whom you are feeding? When you make love, who you are that do it? When you are in company, when you exercise, when you talk, do you not know that you are feeding a god, exercising a god? You carry God about with you, poor wretch, and you do not know it. Do you think I mean some god of silver or gold, outside you? You carry him within yourself, and you do not notice that you are defiling him with unclean thoughts and filthy acts. If an image of God were present, you would not dare do any of the things you do. But when God himself is present within you, and watches over everything and hears everything, are you not ashamed to be thinking and doing these things, you who are blind to your own nature and under the anger of God?

LXI. Then why are we afraid, when we send a young man out of the school to do some business, that he will do something wrong, eat wrongly, make love wrongly, that rags will humble him or fine clothes puff him up? This man does not know his own god; he does not know whom he is setting out with. Can we bear to hear him say, "I wish I had you with me"? Do you not have God there? And having him, do you look for anyone else? Will he tell you anything different from this? If you were a statue by Phidias, his Athena or his Zeus, you would remember both yourself and the artist, and if you had any perception you would try to do nothing unworthy of the one who made you or of yourself, and not to be seen in an unbecoming pose by those who look at you. But as it is, because Zeus made you, do you not care what kind of person you show yourself to be? And yet how is the one artist like the other, or the one work like the other? What work of an artist has in itself, from the start, the powers its making displays? Is it not stone, or bronze, or gold, or ivory? The Athena of Phidias, once she has stretched out her hand and received the Victory upon it, stands that way for all time. But the works of God move, and breathe, and use impressions, and judge them. You are the work of this maker, and do you disgrace it? What? He not only made you but trusted you to yourself alone and put you in your own charge; will you not remember even that, but disgrace your guardianship as well? If God had put an orphan in your charge, would you neglect him so? He has handed you over to yourself, and says, "I had no one more trustworthy than you. Keep this man for me as he was born to be: self-respecting, trustworthy, high-minded, undismayed, free of passion, untroubled." That is how I will show myself to you: trustworthy, self-respecting, noble, untroubled. "Immortal too, then, and ageless, and never sick?" No, but one who dies like a god, who bears sickness like a god.
LXII. Diogenes says that no labor is good unless its aim is courage and strength of soul, and not of body.

LXIII. A guide, when he finds a man who has lost his way, leads him to the right road; he does not laugh at him or abuse him and then walk off. You too, show the man the truth, and you will see that he follows. But as long as you do not show him, do not laugh at him; feel your own inability instead.

LXIV. Now this was the first and most characteristic thing about Socrates: he never lost his temper in an argument, never said anything abusive, never anything insulting, but put up with those who abused him and brought the fight to an end. If you want to know how much power he had in this, read Xenophon's Symposium, and you will see how many fights he broke up. That is why, among the poets too, it is rightly spoken of with the highest praise: "And quickly, with skill, he put an end even to a great quarrel." What then? The business is not very safe now, especially in Rome. For the man who does it clearly must not do it in a corner. He must go up to some man of consular rank, perhaps, or some rich man, and ask him, "You there, can you tell me to whom you have entrusted your horses?" "I can." "To just anyone, a man who knows nothing about horses?" "Certainly not." "Well, and to whom your gold, or your silver, or your clothes?" "Not to just anyone either." "And your body: have you ever considered entrusting it to someone to take care of?" "Of course." "To a man of experience, clearly, in training or in medicine?" "Certainly." "Are these the best things you have, or have you something else better than all of them?" "What do you mean?" "The thing, by Zeus, that uses these, and tests each of them, and deliberates." "You mean the soul?" "You have understood me rightly; that is just what I mean." "By Zeus, I think this is far better than anything else I possess." "Can you tell me, then, in what way you have taken care of your soul? For it is not likely that a man as wise as you, and so well thought of in the city, would carelessly and at random let the best thing he has be neglected and ruined." "Certainly not." "But have you taken care of it yourself? Did you learn how from someone, or find out for yourself?" And here comes the danger: first, that he may say, "What is it to you, my good man? Are you my master?" and then, if you keep on bothering him, that he may lift his fist and hit you. I was once keen on this practice myself, before I fell into these troubles.
LXV. When a young man was boasting in the theater and saying, "I am wise, for I have talked with many wise men," Epictetus said, "And I have talked with many rich men, but I am not rich."

LXVI. We see, then, that the carpenter becomes a carpenter by learning certain things, and the helmsman becomes a helmsman by learning certain things. Perhaps here too, then, it is not enough to want to become a good and noble man; one must also learn certain things. So we ask what they are. The philosophers say that the first thing to learn is this: that there is a God, and that he takes thought for the whole, and that nothing can be hidden from him, not only what we do but even what we intend or think. Next, what the gods are like. For whatever they are found to be, the man who would please and obey them must try, as far as he can, to make himself like them. If the divine is trustworthy, he too must be trustworthy; if free, he too must be free; if generous, he too must be generous; if great-minded, he too must be great-minded; and so, as one who strives to be like God, he must do and say everything that follows.

LXVII. If I show you, then, that you lack the things most necessary and most important for happiness, and that up to now you have taken care of everything except what you should; and if I add the finishing touch, that you do not know what God is, or what man is, or what good is, or what evil: the rest you could perhaps put up with, but that you do not know your own self, how can you put up with me, and stand the proof, and stay? You cannot. You go off at once, offended. And yet what harm have I done you? None, unless the mirror harms the ugly man by showing him what he looks like; unless the doctor insults the sick man when he tells him, "Man, you think nothing is wrong with you, but you have a fever. Eat nothing today; drink water." And no one says, "What an outrageous insult!" But if you tell a man, "Your desires are inflamed, your aversions are low, your purposes contradict each other, your impulses are out of tune with nature, your opinions are careless and false," he goes straight out and says, "He insulted me."

LXVIII. Our life is like what happens at a fair. Cattle and oxen are brought to be sold, and most of the people come either to buy or to sell. But a few come to look at the fair: how it is run, and why, and who set it up, and for what purpose. It is the same here, in this fair. Some, like cattle, trouble themselves about nothing but fodder; for all of you who busy yourselves with property and land and slaves and offices of one kind or another, these things are nothing but fodder. But there are a few at the fair who love to look on. "What, then, is the universe, and who governs it? No one? And how can it be that a city or a household cannot last even a short time without someone to govern it and take care of it, and yet this structure, so great and so beautiful, is kept in such good order at random and by chance? So there is one who governs it. What is he like, and how does he govern? And we, who are we that he has made, and for what work? Do we have some tie to him, some relationship, or none?" That is what happens to these few; and from then on they give their time to this one thing, to study the fair before they leave. What then? They are laughed at by the many; just as, at the other fair, the spectators are laughed at by the traders. And if the cattle had any understanding, they would laugh at those who admire anything but fodder.

divergences.phrase: τὸν ἄνθρωπον ποιήσει λέγειν σοι ταῦτα, ἵν' ἀγνοῇς τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ δαιμονίου
divergences.older: "will He not cause the man to say these words to thee, that thou mayest know the power of the Divine" (Crossley, from an emended text: οὐ ποιήσει … ἵνα γνῷς)
divergences.lectio: "will you make out that it is the man who is saying these things to you, so as to stay ignorant of the power of the divine"
divergences.note: Schenkl keeps the manuscript: ἵν' ἀγνοῇς, "so that you may not know". That gives sense if ποιήσει is second person ("will you make it the man who speaks"), an indignant question, and that is how Lectio takes it. Crossley's version needs two changes to the Greek. Either way the point is the same: the voice is God's, not Epictetus's.

divergences.lectio: "And that is how he wrecked his case."
divergences.note: καταστρέφειν is to overturn. Epictetus goes on, outside Crossley's extract, "What was the need? Only do not plead; do not add 'and I am not pleading'": the story is told against Heraclitus's bravado, not in praise of it.

divergences.lectio: Crossley's two sayings put into current English
divergences.note: These two are among the fragments Schweighäuser collected from the late anthologies. Schenkl's edition, the Greek used for this draft, does not print them, and no Greek for them was to hand. They are Schweighäuser's fragments 57 and 170. The two paragraphs are made from Crossley's English, checked against George Long's independent version of the same fragments (1877), which agrees; in LXII Long reports the Greek word behind "strength" as τόνος, tension or tone. They need the Greek before the edition is called ready.
